summary: Defines an IMAP extension to replace an existing message in a store with a new message, useful for clients that save drafts as a user types.

eli5.summary: Instead of throwing away your old draft and adding a new one, you swap the old page for a new page in one move.

questions: how to update a draft over imap
subtitle: An IMAP command that swaps one stored message for a new one in a single step, built for saving drafts as you type.

tldr.problem: Base IMAP has no replace function, so clients must issue APPEND, STORE and EXPUNGE in turn. An interruption can leave stray or half-finished messages, and APPEND can fail on quota even though the later steps would free space.
tldr.mechanism: The REPLACE and UID REPLACE commands append the new message to a named mailbox and remove the old one so that the change appears to the client as a single action.
tldr.outcome: Clients that auto-save drafts avoid intermediate states and wasted quota, and servers can implement the operation efficiently, ideally as an atomic one.

today: RFC 8508 is a Proposed Standard and, according to the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the definition of the IMAP REPLACE extension.

sections.title: Why Replace Needs Its Own Command
sections.content:
RFC 8508 extends IMAP (RFC 3501) with a new REPLACE command and a UID REPLACE form. Message replacement is common for clients that automatically save drafts or notes as a user composes them.

Base IMAP has no replace function, so clients have used three commands one after another: APPEND, STORE and EXPUNGE. Pipelining them is not recommended, because if one fails the later ones should not run, or the original message could be lost.

The sequence is not atomic. An interruption can leave messages in intermediate states that other clients can see and act on, or strand older revisions and waste quota. APPEND can also fail over quota even though the later steps would free enough room.
sections.eli5: Editing a draft the old way is like writing a fresh page, then tearing out the old one in separate steps. If something interrupts you, both pages may be left in the notebook.

sections.title: What REPLACE Does
sections.content:
In its simplest form, REPLACE is a single-command version of APPEND, STORE +flags \DELETED and UID EXPUNGE for one message, without the quota effects or intermediate states of the three-command sequence. Server developers are encouraged to implement it as an atomic operation.

Servers that support it list REPLACE in the CAPABILITY response. The command takes a message identifier (sequence number, or UID for UID REPLACE), a named mailbox, an optional flag list, an optional date/time string and a message literal.

Servers MUST NOT infer any inheritance of content, flags or annotations from the message being replaced, and MUST NOT generate a response code for the STORE portion.
sections.eli5: REPLACE is a single swap: put the new page in, take the old page out, and nobody ever sees a notebook with both or neither.

sections.title: Semantics and Errors
sections.content:
The new message literal is appended to the named mailbox and the specified message is removed from the selected mailbox. The effect equals APPEND, then [UID] STORE +FLAGS.SILENT \DELETED, then UID EXPUNGE. Quota is judged on the net consumption, and the expunge applies only to the specified message, not to everything flagged \Deleted.

Like MOVE (RFC 6851), the intermediate states do not occur and the response codes differ: those for APPEND and EXPUNGE are returned, those for STORE MUST NOT be generated.

On error, the server MUST NOT leave the selected mailbox inconsistent, and any untagged EXPUNGE MUST NOT be sent until all actions succeed. The result is OK on success, NO if the old message cannot be removed or the new one cannot be added, and BAD if the command is unknown or arguments invalid.

The named mailbox need not be the selected one. For example, a message in the \Drafts mailbox can be replaced with a message in the \Sent mailbox after submission.
sections.eli5: If anything goes wrong halfway, the mailbox is left exactly as it was, and the old message is only removed after the new one is safely in.

sections.title: Interaction with Other Extensions
sections.content:
Because REPLACE resembles APPEND, extensions that affect APPEND affect REPLACE the same way. It is valid only in the selected state, since it works on sequence numbers, and the UID form is likewise not usable from the authenticated state.

  • ACL (RFC 4314): UID REPLACE needs the union of the rights for UID STORE and UID EXPUNGE in the current mailbox and APPEND in the target.
  • CATENATE (RFC 4469): servers supporting both MUST accept CATENATE elements with REPLACE, which can make message editing efficient, for example reusing a large attachment already stored.
  • UIDPLUS (RFC 4315): servers SHOULD send APPENDUID, and are advised to send it in an untagged OK before the EXPUNGE.
  • CONDSTORE/QRESYNC (RFC 7162): the old message is treated as removed by UID EXPUNGE.
  • OBJECTID (RFC 8474): the old and new messages MUST get different EMAILIDs, except when their immutable content is identical.
  • MULTIAPPEND (RFC 3502): no interaction; replacing several messages at once is not defined.
sections.eli5: REPLACE plays well with other IMAP add-ons, and the RFC says for each one what the server has to do so everyone stays in sync.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC believes the extension adds no security problems beyond those already in base IMAP. REPLACE may even prevent some, because it avoids intermediate message states that an attacker could possibly exploit.

IANA added REPLACE to the IMAP Capabilities registry. The formal syntax adds replace = "REPLACE" SP seq-number SP mailbox append-message, and the UID form "UID" SP replace.
sections.eli5: Swapping in one move leaves fewer half-finished moments for a sneaky person to take advantage of.
